What moves the WTI crude oil price

WTI (West Texas Intermediate) crude is the US benchmark oil grade, priced at Cushing, Oklahoma. It is lighter and sweeter than Brent crude (the international benchmark) and typically trades at a small discount to Brent, though the spread can widen significantly during supply gluts or pipeline bottlenecks in the US interior.

OPEC+ production decisions are the single most powerful recurring driver of oil prices. The group, which includes OPEC members and aligned non-OPEC producers led by Russia, collectively controls roughly 40% of global crude production. When OPEC+ cuts output, supply tightens and prices tend to rise. When it increases quotas or member compliance weakens, prices tend to fall. In 2023–2024, Saudi Arabia made unilateral voluntary cuts to support prices while other members produced above quotas, creating tension within the alliance.

US shale production is the key structural counterweight to OPEC+ pricing power. The Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico has driven extraordinary growth in US crude output since 2010, making the United States the world's largest oil producer by 2019. US shale wells have short lead times compared to conventional fields — production can respond to price signals within 6–12 months — which means the US shale industry effectively acts as a cap on oil prices at levels that make new drilling economically attractive (currently estimated around $60–70 per barrel for marginal Permian wells).

Other drivers include geopolitical risk premiums (conflicts in oil-producing regions, sanctions on Iran or Russia, instability in Libya), US dollar strength (oil is priced in dollars globally, so a stronger dollar makes oil more expensive for non-dollar buyers and can reduce demand), weekly EIA inventory reports (which signal whether US supply-demand balance is tightening or loosening), and seasonal demand patterns (summer driving season in the US, winter heating demand in the Northern Hemisphere).

Oil and gold: the macro relationship

Gold and oil share a US dollar pricing convention and a sensitivity to inflation expectations, but they diverge in important ways. Oil is a consumed commodity — every barrel burned is gone. Gold is a stored commodity — almost all gold ever mined still exists above ground. Oil demand is being structurally altered by the energy transition toward electric vehicles and renewables. Gold demand is supported by central bank reserve accumulation, which is accelerating as a trend as countries outside the Western bloc diversify away from US dollar reserves. The Gold/Oil ratio on GoldAlert captures this relationship in a single daily number, showing whether gold is historically expensive or cheap relative to oil.
